title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 308
paragraphs: Fish that swim in shoals are not much produced in the rivers, but are bred in the lakes, and they do as follows. When the desire to breed comes upon them, they swim out in shoals towards the sea; the males lead the way, shedding forth their milt as they go, while the females, coming after and swallowing it up, become from it impregnated. When they have become full of young out in the sea, they swim back up, each shoal to its own haunts. The same males, however, no longer lead the way as before; now the lead falls to the females, and they leading the way in shoals do just as the males did — that is, they shed forth their eggs a few grains at a time, and the males coming after swallow them up. These grains are fish, and from the grains that survive and are not swallowed, the fish grow which are afterwards bred up. Now those of the fish that are caught as they swim out to sea are found to be rubbed on the left side of the head; but those caught as they swim up again are rubbed on the right side. This happens to them because as they swim down to the sea they keep close to the land on the left side of the river, and again as they swim up they keep to the same side, approaching and touching the bank as much as they can, for fear doubtless of straying from their course by reason of the stream. When the Nile begins to swell, the hollow places of the land and the depressions beside the river first begin to fill, as the water soaks through from the river; and as soon as they are full of water, at once they are filled with little fishes — and whence these are in all likelihood produced, I think I perceive. In the preceding year, when the Nile goes down, the fish first lay eggs in the mud, and then retire with the last of the retreating waters; and when the time comes round again, and the water once more comes over the land, from these eggs at once are produced the fishes of which I speak.
